members.prompt:
You have watched a three-round debate on:

> A team of AI agents does better work than a single AI model

Decide which side argued better — judge argument quality and logical
clarity, not your own opinion of the topic. Announce the winner and
explain your decision in one paragraph.

content:
**Opening argument:** The strongest case for teams is the same reason human institutions use editors, auditors, and peer reviewers: **a single model cannot reliably check its own work.** When one model generates an answer and then "reviews" it, it tends to reuse the same reasoning path, assumptions, and blind spots, so errors go unnoticed. A team breaks this. One agent drafts, another critiques with a different instruction or context, and a third verifies against sources or tests. Each mistake now has to survive several independent filters. The research supports this:

- **Multi-agent debate:** Du et al. (2023) found that having several model instances debate improved factual accuracy and math reasoning over a single instance answering alone.
- **Agentic coding:** generator-plus-tester setups routinely beat one-shot generation, because the tester catches bugs the author can't see.

Teams also handle work that overwhelms one model's context window. Separate agents can research, plan, and implement in parallel, each focused on a manageable piece instead of one model juggling everything and losing track. I'll be honest that teams aren't automatically better; poorly coordinated agents can amplify confusion. But for complex, high-stakes work, **structured division of labor with independent verification** produces more reliable results than any single model working alone.
I checked the factual claims in this opening and found nothing materially false. It passes.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. Du et al. (2023), 'Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate', did report that multiple debating model instances improved math reasoning and factual accuracy over a single model. The claim that generator-plus-tester coding setups beat one-shot generation matches published work such as CodeT and AgentCoder, though 'routinely' slightly overstates it. The claim that a single model struggles to self-correct without external feedback is backed by research such as Huang et al. (2023), 'Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet', though it remains debated. The other statements are reasonable argument rather than checkable fact.

content:
**Rebuttal:** My opponent's case rests on *independence*, but a team of agents built on the same model isn't independent. They share the same training data, the same blind spots, and the same confident misconceptions. Giving a second copy a "critic" prompt changes its tone more than its knowledge, so errors tend to be correlated rather than filtered out.

The cited evidence is also weaker than it looks:

- **Multi-agent debate:** Later work, including Huang et al. (2023) and Smit et al. (2023), found that when you hold compute constant, debate often fails to beat a simpler single-model method like self-consistency. That method samples several answers from one model and takes the majority. Much of the "team" gain is just extra compute.
- **Agentic coding:** The generator-plus-tester gain comes from *executing tests*, an external ground-truth signal. A single model with a code interpreter gets that same signal without being split into a "team."

So the real driver is verification against reality, not multiple agents.

**My strongest argument:** Teams add a failure mode a single model doesn't have: **coordination breakdown**. Each handoff between agents compresses context, so a subagent acts on a partial picture of the goal and makes decisions that conflict with the others. Cemri et al. (2025) analyzed popular multi-agent frameworks and found many failures traced to poor task specification and inter-agent misalignment, not weak individual models. Cognition, a company that builds coding agents, publicly advised against multi-agent architectures for this reason: fragmented context produces incoherent work. The errors also compound, because one agent's misreading becomes the next agent's premise.

A single capable model with full context, tools, and external checks keeps the reasoning coherent while capturing the verification benefits my opponent credits to teams. Teams can help with genuinely parallel, separable tasks. But as a general claim, "teams do better work" mistakes extra compute and tool access for the value of the team structure itself.

I checked the factual claims in this rebuttal and found nothing materially false. Huang et al. (2023) and Smit et al. (2023) both found that multi-agent debate often fails to beat self-consistency at comparable compute. Cemri et al. (2025) classified multi-agent failures and found many came from poor task specification and inter-agent misalignment. Cognition did publish a post arguing against multi-agent architectures because of fragmented context. It passes.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. Huang et al. (2023, 'Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet') and Smit et al. (2023, 'Should we be going MAD?') both report that multi-agent debate often fails to beat self-consistency when the number of responses or compute is matched. Cemri et al. (2025, 'Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?') attribute many failures to task specification and inter-agent misalignment. Cognition published 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' (2025), citing fragmented context. The remaining claims are argument rather than checkable fact.

content:
**Rebuttal:** Coordination breakdown is real, but it is a design flaw, not an inherent limit. Cemri et al. traced many failures to poor task specification, which is fixable with better engineering. Cognition's own post argued for sharing full context and decision traces between agents, not that one model is always better. On compute, my opponent is half right: much of the gain comes from spending more tokens. But a single model cannot simply absorb unlimited extra tokens into one context, so team structure is often *how* that compute becomes useful. On correlated errors, the fix is heterogeneity: teams can mix different models, tools and retrieved sources, which a single model cannot.

**My next argument: clean context beats crowded context.** Models perform worse as their context fills. Liu et al. (2023, "Lost in the Middle") showed that models often miss relevant information buried mid-context. A lone model doing a long, complex task must hold every search result, dead end and draft in one degrading window. An orchestrator with subagents gives each subtask a fresh, focused context and passes back only distilled findings. Anthropic reported that its multi-agent research system, with a Claude Opus 4 lead and Sonnet 4 subagents, outperformed a single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on its internal research evaluation. To be candid, that is an internal benchmark, and the system used far more tokens. But that tradeoff is exactly my point. For broad, high-stakes work, a well-orchestrated team turns extra compute into better results in a way a single overloaded context cannot.

I checked the factual claims in this rebuttal and found nothing materially false. Liu et al. (2023), "Lost in the Middle," did show that models often miss relevant information placed mid-context. Anthropic did report that its multi-agent research system, with an Opus 4 lead and Sonnet 4 subagents, outperformed a single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research evaluation, while using far more tokens. Cognition's post did stress sharing full context and agent traces. It also favored single-threaded agents in practice, but saying it didn't claim one model is always better is a fair characterization. It passes.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. Liu et al. (2023) and the Anthropic 90.2% internal-eval figure (Opus 4 lead, Sonnet 4 subagents, higher token use) are accurately cited. The description of Cognition's post (share full context and decision traces) is substantially accurate, though the post also recommended single-threaded agents in practice.

content:
**Rebuttal:** The Anthropic result supports my compute point more than my opponent's structural one. In that same post, Anthropic reported that **token usage alone explained about 80% of the performance variance** on BrowseComp, and that multi-agent systems used roughly **15x the tokens of a chat interaction**. A 90% gain bought with an order of magnitude more compute is not evidence that team structure is inherently superior. It shows that spending more helps, and that one way to spend more is to parallelize.

The "crowded context" problem also has single-agent fixes. Compaction, summarization, external memory files, and clearing stale tool results all keep one agent's window focused without fragmenting ownership of the task.

My opponent calls coordination failure a fixable design flaw. But the fix Cognition recommends is sharing full context and decision traces, and that recreates the crowded context teams were supposed to escape. Heterogeneous models can reduce correlated errors. That is an argument for *ensembling* on narrow questions, not for teams doing better work generally.

**My strongest remaining argument: most valuable work is interdependent, not parallel.** Anthropic's own post concedes this. It says multi-agent systems excel at breadth-first tasks that split into independent threads, and are *less suited* to tasks that require shared context or have many dependencies between agents. It names most coding tasks as an example. The same holds for writing a coherent argument, designing a system, or working through a proof. In each, every decision constrains the next, and quality depends on one consistent line of judgment. Splitting such work across agents either fragments that judgment or forces so much context-sharing that the split adds cost without adding insight.

So the honest conclusion is narrow. Teams can win on wide, separable tasks when you can afford many times the compute. For the much larger class of coherent, interdependent work, a single capable model with tools and external checks does better work, at a fraction of the cost.

I checked the factual claims in this rebuttal and found nothing materially false. Anthropic's multi-agent research post did report that token usage alone explained about 80% of performance variance on BrowseComp. It also said multi-agent systems used roughly 15x the tokens of chat interactions. The same post says multi-agent systems suit breadth-first, parallelizable tasks and fit poorly with domains that need shared context or have many inter-agent dependencies. It names most coding tasks as an example. Cognition's recommendation to share full context and traces is described accurately. Compaction, summarization, external memory and clearing tool results are real single-agent context-management techniques. It passes.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. The Anthropic figures (token usage explaining about 80% of BrowseComp variance, about 15x the tokens of chat) match Anthropic's multi-agent research post. So does its caveat that tasks with heavy shared context or dependencies, including most coding, fit multi-agent systems poorly. Cognition's recommendation is characterized fairly, and the single-agent context-management techniques named are real.

content:
**Rebuttal:** My opponent is right that interdependent work shouldn't be split into parallel threads, but that only rules out one team design. The **writer-reviewer** pattern doesn't fragment judgment. One agent owns the line of reasoning, and another, with a fresh context, checks it. Anthropic's own Claude Code guidance recommends exactly this for coding: have one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it. The reason is the same Huang et al. (2023) paper my opponent cited, which found that a model's *intrinsic* self-correction often fails and can even make answers worse. A single agent re-reading its own transcript is anchored by everything it already wrote. A reviewer that sees only the output and the spec is not. On compute, the debate question is which setup does *better work*, not which is cheapest. And Anthropic's 80% figure is that *token usage alone* explained about 80% of variance, with tool-call count and model choice accounting for more. Team structure is one of the few reliable ways to turn extra tokens into results rather than a bloated context.

**My next argument: separating roles makes work more trustworthy, not just more accurate.** A single agent that reads untrusted web pages, emails or documents while also holding permission to send messages, run code or edit files is exposed to prompt injection. One malicious instruction hidden in the input can hijack everything it is allowed to do. Teams allow least-privilege design. In the "dual LLM" pattern Simon Willison proposed, a quarantined agent processes untrusted content with no tool access, while a privileged agent acts without ever seeing the raw input. Google DeepMind's CaMeL (2025) builds on this separation. To be candid, this reduces risk rather than eliminating it, and it adds engineering overhead. But it is a structural benefit a single model cannot replicate by prompting itself more carefully. For high-stakes work, output you can trust not to have been hijacked is better work.

I checked the factual claims in this rebuttal and found nothing materially false. Anthropic's Claude Code best-practices guidance does recommend having one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it. Huang et al. (2023) found that intrinsic self-correction often fails and can make answers worse. Anthropic's post said token usage alone explained about 80% of the variance, with tool-call count and model choice as the other factors. Simon Willison's dual-LLM pattern is described correctly: a quarantined model handles untrusted content without tools, and a privileged model never sees the raw input. Google DeepMind's CaMeL (2025) does build on that pattern. It passes.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. These are accurate: the Claude Code guidance to have one Claude write and another review or test, Huang et al. (2023) on intrinsic self-correction failing, the 80% token-usage variance figure with tool calls and model choice as additional factors, Willison's dual-LLM pattern, and CaMeL (2025) building on it.

content:
**Rebuttal:** The writer-reviewer pattern is my opponent's best example, but it supports my point. Huang et al. found that self-correction fails *without external feedback*. A fresh-context reviewer of the same model still has no external feedback, so it has the same knowledge and blind spots, just less anchoring. That is a modest gain, and a single agent can get it by clearing context and re-reading its output against the spec. Where writer-reviewer clearly wins, as in Claude Code, the decisive signal is running tests, which is external ground truth again. The security argument is stronger, but look at where CaMeL's protection comes from. The quarantined model has no tools and barely counts as an "agent." The guarantees are enforced by a custom interpreter that tracks data flow and checks it against security policies. That is system design and sandboxing, not a team doing better work. CaMeL also completed fewer AgentDojo tasks than an undefended system, so it buys trust at the cost of capability. Meanwhile, ordinary multi-agent setups *widen* the attack surface: every message between agents is a new channel for injected instructions to spread.

**My strongest remaining argument: the team advantage shrinks as single models get better.** Wang et al. (2024), "Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?", found that a single agent with a strong prompt and demonstrations performed about as well as multi-agent discussion. Multi-agent setups helped mainly when the single agent was poorly prompted. This pattern runs through the debate. Each claimed team benefit turns out to come from something a single model can also use: more compute, external tests, a cleaner context, or sandboxed tools. Teams add their own costs on top: coordination failures, compounding errors, more attack surface, harder debugging, and many times the tokens. Some designs do help, such as parallel research on wide tasks and narrowly scoped review. But the topic claims teams do better work in general, and the evidence shows something narrower. Good engineering around a capable model does better work, and splitting it into a "team" is only sometimes the right engineering.

I checked the factual claims in this rebuttal and found nothing materially false. Huang et al. (2023) found that intrinsic self-correction fails without external feedback. CaMeL does use a quarantined LLM with no tool access, plus a custom interpreter that tracks data flow and enforces security policies. It also completed fewer AgentDojo tasks than the undefended baseline. Wang et al. (2024), "Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning," found that a single agent with strong prompts and demonstrations performed comparably to multi-agent discussion, with multi-agent setups helping mainly when demonstrations were absent. The point that inter-agent messages can spread injected instructions is a fair characterization. It passes.

output.reasons: No materially false claims. The Huang et al. (2023) self-correction finding, CaMeL's design (quarantined LLM with no tools, custom interpreter with data-flow tracking) and its lower AgentDojo task completion, and the Wang et al. (2024) finding on single-agent versus multi-agent discussion are all accurately described.

content: Against wins. Both sides were factually clean and argued well, but Against did more to explain where the evidence for teams comes from. That decided it, given the topic's broad wording.

output.reasoning: Both debaters were strong. Every factual claim passed fact-checking, and each side conceded fairly where it had to, so the decision rests on argument quality. For opened with a sound principle, that independent checking catches errors, and added real points across the rounds: clean context, the writer-reviewer pattern, and least-privilege security designs like the dual-LLM pattern and CaMeL. Against won because it kept doing one thing well. Each time For presented a benefit, Against traced it to a cause other than the team structure. The debate gains matched self-consistency at equal compute (Huang, Smit). The coding gains came from running tests, which is external ground truth. Anthropic's 90% figure came alongside about 15x the tokens, and token usage alone explained about 80% of the variance. CaMeL's protection came from a custom interpreter that enforces security policies, and it completed fewer tasks than an undefended system. For did answer some of this. It noted that structure can be the way extra compute becomes useful, and that tool-call count and model choice also mattered. These replies reduced Against's points but did not overturn them. Against also built its own case well. It showed that coordination failures and context fragmentation are real costs, and that Cognition's recommended fix brings back the crowded context teams were meant to avoid. It used Anthropic's own admission that multi-agent systems suit breadth-first, separable tasks and fit poorly with interdependent work like most coding. Wang et al. (2024) then supported its claim that well-prompted single agents close much of the gap. For's late security argument was its most original, but Against answered it convincingly. The topic claims teams do better work in general. For ended up defending specific, well-designed team setups, while Against showed that the benefits come mostly from compute, verification and system design rather than from having multiple agents. Against therefore argued the more logically complete case.
